edges.effect_quant: Pet ownership tracks with slightly better cardiovascular profiles in some pooled analyses, but the adjusted disease-level signal is weak and inconsistent.
edges.mechanism: Living with a pet may increase daily movement, lower perceived loneliness, and blunt stress reactivity, all of which could nudge cardiovascular risk in a favorable direction. The main limitation is that these pathways are deeply confounded by baseline health, income, housing, and social support, so observational estimates can easily exaggerate a true causal effect.
edges.summary: The cleanest reading is that pet ownership may help cardiovascular health a little, but the case is far from decisive. Meta-analyses report small favorable shifts in blood pressure and cardiovascular mortality in some subgroups, yet the broader adjusted association with incident cardiovascular disease often shrinks toward null.
edges.caveats: This evidence is observational and highly vulnerable to healthy-owner bias. Effects may differ by species, baseline disease status, and whether the apparent benefit reflects dog walking rather than pet ownership itself.
